en: Peṭakopadesa 1.
The First Stage: Exposition of the Noble Truths.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Homage to the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the seers of the ultimate truth, who have reached perfection in the virtues of morality and the rest.
There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view in a disciple:
the voice of another that leads to the truth, and wise attention within oneself.
In this context, what is "the voice of another"?
It is the teaching, instruction, admonition, truthful discourse, and that which accords with truth from another.
[It consists of] the four truths:
Suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path. The teaching, the pointing out, the revealing, the analyzing, the making plain, and the elucidation of these four truths—
this is called the "voice in accordance with the truths."
In this context, what is wise attention directed inwardly?
Wise attention directed inwardly means that which, regarding the Dhamma as it has been taught, does not project the object outwardly, but is wise attention;
this is called wise attention.
That mode is the methodical way, the door, the procedure, and the means.
Just as a man, by rubbing dry wood that is free from sap with a dry upper fire-stick on a dry surface, is capable of attaining light. Why is that?
For the attainment of the fire through systematic method.
In the same way, when one attends to the teaching on the dharma that is non-erroneous regarding the origin, cessation, and path of suffering—
this is called systematic attention.
Just as three similes, never heard before and unheard of previously, occur to me:
"Whoever is not free from lust for sensual pleasures... [and so on]...
"Two similes are to be applied inappropriately; what was stated regarding the latter ones [is as follows]."
In this context, the voice of another and internal wise attention—
these are the two conditions.
The wisdom that arises by means of the voice of another—
This is called wisdom born of hearing.
That wisdom which arises through wise attention directed inwardly is called wisdom born of reflection.
These two kinds of wisdom are to be understood,
as well as the two preceding conditions.
These two causes and two conditions lead to the arising of right view in a disciple.
In this regard, it is impossible that one who does not understand the meaning of the voice of another teaching the sequence of the Truths will experience the meaning;
nor is it possible that one who does not experience the meaning will attend to it wisely.
It is indeed possible that one who understands the meaning of the voice of another teaching the sequence of the Truths will experience the meaning.
"It is possible that one who experiences the meaning will attend to it wisely.
This is the cause, this is the object, this is the means for a disciple’s deliverance; there is no other.
This [attainment] is neither conjoined with the simultaneous understanding of the Sutta’s meaning, nor with the pursuit of the sound from another."
One who does not understand the meaning cannot attain the superhuman state, the knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones;
therefore, one who desires to attain Nibbāna should seek the meanings by means of what consists of learning.
In that regard, this is the successive order for seeking them: the sixteen modes of conveying, the five guides, and the eighteen root-terms.
In this regard, there is this summary verse:
"The Guide has sixteen bases,
five methods, and the investigation of the Teaching."
The eighteen root-terms have been pointed out by the lineage of Kaccāyana.
In that regard, what are the sixteen modes of conveying meaning?

Exposition, investigation, reasoning, proximate cause, characteristic, fourfold array, turning back, analysis, reversal, synonym, designation, entry, cleansing, resolution, equipment, and coordination—
these are the sixteen modes of conveying meaning (*hāra*).
Regarding this, there is a summary verse:
Exposition, investigation, reasoning,
proximate cause, characteristic,
the fourfold array, and turning back.
The transformation of grammatical cases,
synonyms, designations,
the methods of entry, and the means of purification;
The foundation, the requisites,
and the sixteen applications.
In this regard, what are the five methods?
The *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*, the *Tipukkhalo*, the *Sīhavikkīḷita*, the *Disālocana*, and the *Aṅkusa*.
Therein, the summary verse (*uddānagāthā*) is:
"The first is the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*..."
And the second is Tipukkhalo;
the third is named Sīhavikkīḷita— such is the method.
They say "Direction-observation" is the first,
"The fourth mark of the method" is the second,
and the fifth is named "The Hook."
All five methods have been traversed.
In this regard, what are the eighteen root-terms?
Ignorance, craving, greed, hatred, delusion, perception of beauty, perception of pleasure, perception of permanence, perception of self, serenity, and insight.
Non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, the perception of foulness, the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self—these are the eighteen root-terms.
Among them, nine terms are unwholesome, wherein all that is unwholesome converges;
nine terms are wholesome, wherein all that is wholesome converges.
What are the nine unwholesome factors wherein all that is unwholesome converges?
Ignorance up to the perception of self—these are the nine unwholesome factors wherein all that is unwholesome converges.
What are the nine wholesome factors wherein all that is wholesome converges?
From serenity up to the perception of non-self—these nine terms are wholesome, wherein all that is wholesome converges.
These are the eighteen root terms.
Regarding this, there are these summary verses:
Craving and ignorance, greed,
hatred, and likewise delusion;
and the four perversions—
The Ground of Defilements consists of nine terms:
the foundations of mindfulness, serenity,
insight, and the roots of wholesomeness.
All this is wholesome;
the Chapter on the Faculties consists of nine terms.
All that is wholesome is connected with these nine terms.
And the unwholesome [consciousness] consists of nine;
in the single [categories], there are nine root-terms,
and in both together, eighteen root-terms.
Of these eighteen root terms, those nine terms that are unwholesome are the origin of suffering;
those nine terms that are wholesome are the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Thus, suffering is the fruit of the origin, and cessation is the fruit of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
These four noble truths were taught by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī.

Therein, for the purpose of announcing, proclaiming, revealing, analyzing, clarifying, and establishing this very same meaning, immeasurable syllables, phrases, phonemes, modes, linguistic expressions, and expositions have been taught regarding the noble truth of suffering.

Thus, for all these truths, each individual truth is to be sought out through immeasurable expressions, phrases, syllables, modes, designations, and explanations; and that expression exists both through the multiplicity of meanings and through the multiplicity of expressions.

For whatever ascetic or brahmin should say, "Rejecting this suffering, I shall proclaim another suffering," his statement would be devoid of a factual basis, and when questioned, he would not be able to substantiate it.
Such is the case with the truths.
Whatever was spoken by the Blessed One during the interval between the night he attained full enlightenment and the night he attained final Nibbāna through non-clinging—
whether it be a discourse (sutta), a mixed prose and verse (geyya), an exposition (veyyākaraṇa), a verse (gāthā), an inspired utterance (udāna),
a traditional saying (itivuttaka), a birth story (jātaka), a marvelous account (abbhutadhamma), or an analytical discussion (vedalla)— all that is the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.

There is nothing outside the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) in the Dhamma-teachings of the Blessed Buddhas; therefore, every such discourse should be sought among the Noble Teachings (*ariyadhamma*).
In that regard, these four Noble Truths, which possess the nature of light, are stable for thorough comprehension.
Therein, what is suffering (*dukkha*)?
Birth, aging, sickness, and death—in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Herein, this is the description of their characteristics: birth has the characteristic of manifestation; aging has the characteristic of maturation;

sickness has the characteristic of the nature of painful suffering; death has the characteristic of passing away; sorrow has the characteristic of tormenting through separation from the beloved and through change; lamentation has the characteristic of wailing.
Lamentation; suffering, characterized by physical oppression; grief, characterized by mental oppression; despair, characterized by the burning of the defilements;

association with the unpleasant, characterized by the encounter with what is disagreeable; separation from the pleasant, characterized by the loss of what is agreeable; non-attainment, characterized by the frustration of one's intentions;
the five aggregates of clinging, characterized by lack of full understanding; and aging-and-death, characterized by the ripening and decay of conditioned things.
Old age and death have the characteristic of manifestation and passing away; death and rebirth have the characteristic of the production of rebirth-linking.

Origination has the characteristic of producing rebirth-linking; cessation has the characteristic of completely abandoning origination; the path has the characteristic of uprooting underlying tendencies.
Suffering has the characteristic of illness; origination has the characteristic of perceiving; the path has the characteristic of leading out; cessation has the characteristic of peace.
The Nibbāna-element without residue is characterized by the cessation of the state of non-relinking;
and suffering and its origin, suffering and its cessation, suffering and the path, origin and suffering,
origin and cessation, origin and the path, cessation and origin, cessation and suffering, and cessation...
The path and the path, cessation and the path, origination and the path, and suffering and the path.
Regarding these, there are these discourses:
“That first night... [etc.]”
The young man dwells in the womb;
having already set forth, he goes on,
and as he goes, he does not turn back.
Ānanda, these eight rebirths through giving are the discourse on the single-increment series;
this is birth.
In that regard, what is aging?
“Having lived the holy life without practicing it,
and having failed to acquire wealth in youth,
they brood like aged herons.”
Like a pond whose fish have perished.
There are five portents among the gods:
this is old age.
In this regard, what is illness?
O King, from where could it come to you yourself?
You too have experienced that you are subject to aging.
The Kshatriya is the fruit of his own karma;
for the world does not carry away one's karma.
There are three kinds of illness:
This is illness.
Therein, what is death?
It is just as, for example, with a potter’s...
A clay vessel—
whether small or large,
whether fired or unfired.
Everything ends in dissolution;
such is the life of mortals.
Behold those things cherished as "mine," quivering with agitation.
Just as fish in water whose stream has run dry;
seeing this too, one should wander without "mine-ness," not forming attachment to states of existence.
The Udakappana Sutta—
this is death.
In this context, what is sorrow?
Here he sorrows, and after passing away he sorrows;
the doer of evil sorrows in both places.
He sorrows, he is tormented.
Having seen his own defilement by karma—
the three types of misconduct—
this is sorrow.
In this regard, what is lamentation?
Those who are greedy for sensual pleasures, addicted, deluded,
and incapable of giving, are settled upon the uneven path.
Afflicted by suffering, they lament:
"What shall we become when we have passed away from here?
There are three failures:
This is lamentation.
In that regard, what is suffering?
There were iron spikes for the virtuous.
All are individually conscious;
they are ablaze like fires,
crowded with masses of flames.
"Great indeed is that fever," as stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya within the Saccasaṃyutta:
"This is suffering.
In that context, what is mental grief?
Beset by his own thoughts,
he meditates like a beggar;
having heard the outcry of others, he is distressed.
Such a person becomes dejected.
These two things are to be regretted:
this is mental distress.
In this regard, what is despair?
It is like the furnace of a smith:
it burns within, not without.
Thus my heart burns,
having heard that the lotus has been born.
There are three fires:
This is anguish.
In this context, what is association with the unpleasant?
It is like rust arising from iron itself.
Satisfied, it devours that very person;
so too do one's own deeds lead the one who behaves with excessive license to a state of misery.
These two misrepresent the Tathāgata; this is from the *Ekuttarika* Sutta among the pairs:
this is association with the unpleasant.
In that regard, what is dissociation from the pleasant?
Just as a person who has awakened does not see what was encountered in a dream,
so too one does not see beloved people.
One does not see that deceased person who has passed away.
Having recognized that those gods are subject to falling away, they instruct them with three words.
This is separation from the beloved.
And that which one desires but does not obtain—
O three daughters of Māra— if,
while longing for it, [one is overcome by passion...]
For a person in whom desire has arisen,
those sensual pleasures fade away,
and they suffer as if pierced by an arrow.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
The eye, the ear, and the nose,
the tongue, the body, and then the mind.
These are the terrible worldly baits where ordinary beings dwell. There are,
monks, these five aggregates:
This is suffering.
In this regard, what are aging and death?
Truly, this life is short indeed.
One dies even before a hundred years have passed;
or else, though one lives without hardship,
one nevertheless dies through old age.
In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, in the *Pasenadi Saṃyutta*, there is a discourse: "My grandmother has passed away"—this is aging and death.
In that regard, what is passing away and what is rebirth?
“All beings will die;
for life ends in death.
They will go according to their karma.”
“...reaching the fruits of their own deeds.”—
This is passing away and rebirth.

Having understood suffering through its characteristics by means of these suttas and others similar to them— which have entered into that ninefold collection— one should point out the Noble Truth of Suffering, both common and uncommon.
A verse should be inferred from verses, or an exposition from expositions:
"This is suffering.
In that regard, what is the origin of suffering?
Beings are attached to sensual pleasures, stuck by the attachment to sense-desires;
not seeing the fault in the fetters,
those stuck by the attachment to the fetters will never [be free].
They would cross over a vast and great flood.
The four taints are the sutta;
this is the origin of suffering.
In that regard, what is the cessation of suffering?
It is that in which neither delusion nor pride dwells,
where one is free from greed, without the sense of "mine," and devoid of longing.
With anger dispelled and his self extinguished, he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a bhikkhu.
There are these two kinds of liberation: the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and [the liberation by wisdom].
And the liberation through wisdom by the fading away of ignorance—
this is cessation.
In this regard, what is the path?
This alone is the path, there is no other,
for the purification of vision:
the Noble Eightfold Path.
This is the delusion of Māra.
Monks, these seven factors of enlightenment—
this is the path.
In this regard, what are the four noble truths?
“Of those phenomena that arise from a cause,
the Tathāgata has stated their cause;”
"And their cessation—such is the teaching of the Great Recluse.
Phenomena arise from causes; suffering is the cause, and its origin is the cause—this is the word of the Blessed One.
This is the phenomenon that is cessation: for whoever dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are subject to fetters, their defilements and craving increase;
with craving as condition, clinging arises... and so on...
such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Therein, whatever fetter—
that is the origin.
And those phenomena which are objects of the fetters, as well as sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair that arise— these are suffering.
"This is suffering.
The contemplation of the danger in things that fetter—
one is the path.
One is liberated from birth, aging, diseases, deaths, sorrows, lamentations, and even from despair—
this is Nibbāna.
These are the four truths.
In this regard, what is the Nibbāna-element without residue?
For one who has gone to final rest, there is no measure;
indeed, that by which one might designate him does not exist.
Because all attachments have been utterly eradicated, the wise one remains cool amidst all hundreds of disputes.
(From the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the *Godhika Saṃyutta*).
These are the uncommon discourses.
Wherever the truths are demonstrated, there that meaning should be sought by applying it to the characteristics of the truths through immeasurable modes of expression.

In this regard, the phrasing follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the phrasing; for each of these, there are immeasurable modes of expression. By means of these discourses as they have been set forth, the four noble truths are to be demonstrated.
Verses should be inferred from verses not included in the Five Collections, and prose-expositions from prose-expositions.
These are the unique discourses.
For them, here are the summary verses:
On whatever night one first [attains enlightenment],
there are eight rebirths through giving and five portents.
Like a pond whose fish have perished;
how could there be peace for him, O King?
These three gods are afflicted by illness.
Just as with a potter,
or like the measuring of a river;
one grieves here, and one grieves after passing away.
The three types of misconduct;
those greedy for sensual pleasures and addicted to them,
up to the three failures.
For him there were a hundred iron spikes and a most intense fever;
overcome by his own thoughts, he—
In that regard, by means of the things to be heated,
three fires are illustrated, just like the torches of smiths.
The gods instruct him in three ways regarding the stain that has arisen: false accusations against the Tathāgata.
Like a union in a dream;
even the three daughters of Māra cause him to suffer as if pierced by arrows.
The eye, the ear, and the nose—
these are declared to be the five aggregates;
alas, this life is indeed short.
My grandmother is very old.
All beings will die;
there is arising and passing away.
Beings are bound by sensual pleasures and by the four taints;
in whom no deceit dwells, [therein they do not abide].
These are the two liberations of mind;
this is the path, there is no other,
and the factors of enlightenment are well-taught.
There is no measure for one who has gone to rest;
Godhika has attained final Nibbāna.
Those phenomena that arise from a cause—
Contemplating the fetters.
These are the ten summary verses for them.
Among these, there are the common suttas—in which suttas the truths are taught commonly, whether in direct order, in reverse order, or in a mixed manner.
In this regard, this is the beginning:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance,” [said the Blessed One,] O Ajita.
Through negligence, discernment does not shine forth;
I call craving its defilement,
and suffering its great terror.
Therein, that which is ignorance and craving is the origin;
that which is the great fear is suffering.
These are the two truths.
Suffering and its origin.
“The fetter and the things that are subject to fettering”—this is the exposition in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, in the *Cittasaṃyutta*.
Therein, that which is the fetter is the origin.
Those phenomena that are subject to fetters: this is suffering.
These are two truths:
suffering and its origin.
In this regard, what is suffering and its cessation?
For the bhikkhu who has cut off craving for existence and whose guide has been severed—
The wandering in birth is exhausted;
now there is no further becoming.
That which is mind—this is suffering.
The cutting off of craving for existence is the cessation of suffering;
"the wandering in birth is exhausted, there is now no further becoming"—this is the description.
These are the two truths.
Suffering and its cessation.
Monks, there are these two liberations:
the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.
That which is consciousness is suffering;
that which is liberation is cessation.
These are the two truths.
Suffering and its cessation.
In that regard, what is suffering and the path?
Having understood this body to be like a jar—
Having established this mind as being like a city,
fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom;
guard what has been won, and remain without attachment.
In this context, that which is the body comparable to a jar and the mind comparable to a city is suffering (*dukkha*).
That which is "one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom" is the path (*magga*).
These are the two truths.
“Monks, whatever is not yours should be abandoned.
That which is the fetter is the path.
Those phenomena that are not-self and should be abandoned—form, and so on, up to consciousness—this is both suffering and the path.”
In this regard, what is suffering, its origin, and its cessation?
Whatever sorrows or lamentations there are,
and whatever various forms of suffering exist in the world;
These arise dependent upon the beloved;
when the beloved is absent, these do not come to be.
Whatever sorrow and lamentation there is, and whatever manifold suffering there is—which all arises from affection—this is suffering.
That which is affection is the origin.
The removal of desire and lust for that, the non-performance of what is dear, is the cessation.
These are the three truths.
The wanderer Timbaruka accepts [the view] that "it is both self-made and made by another.
This investigation is suffering.

That middle way which does not approach these two extremes—beginning with "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" up to "conditioned by birth is aging and death"—this too is both suffering and its origin.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—this is suffering.
Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, and clinging—this is the origin.
Thus, one should investigate this as "self-made. That which is suffering within dependent origination is pointed out here as its origin.
With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations, and so on up to the cessation of aging and death—this is cessation.
These three truths are suffering, its origin, and its cessation.
In that regard, what are suffering, its origin, and the path?
“How could a person who has seen suffering and its source bow down to sensual pleasures?
For having understood that sensual pleasures are attachments in the world, [one should not yield to them].”
“Let one who possesses mindfulness train for their restraint.
He who has seen suffering: “This is suffering”;
from what it arises: “this is its origin.”
From the time it is directly perceived until the training for its removal, this is the path.
These are the three truths.
This is the Gopālakopama Sutta from the Ekādasaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
In this context, from the cessation of perception of form up to the six sense bases— just as one covers a wound, just as one reaches a ford,
and just as one obtains sublime joy and gladness connected with the Dhamma— these fourfold bases of individual existence constitute suffering.
As long as one is removing flies, this is the origin (*samudaya*).
The removal of flies through freedom from perceptions of form, the dressing of the wound, knowledge of the path, and skill regarding the pasture—this is the path (*magga*).

All remaining phenomena are causes, conditions, and supports; they include milking with residue and various offerings. Furthermore, due to the condition of having virtuous friends, these phenomena and the knowledge of the path are the cause. These are the three truths.
In this regard, what is suffering, the path, and cessation?
Mindfulness established in the body,
being restrained in the six bases of contact.
A bhikkhu who is constantly concentrated should know Nibbāna for himself.
Therein, both the mindfulness directed to the body and the six sense bases— wherever all this suffering exists— are to be understood.
Mindfulness directed to the body, the restraint of virtue, and the concentration wherein that mindfulness resides—this is the aggregate of wisdom.
The entire aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration constitute the Path.
Nibbāna is to be known by one who dwells in this manner.
This is cessation; these are the three truths.
Being established in virtue, two things are to be developed: serenity and insight.
Therein, those phenomena that are co-nascent with the mind are suffering.
Both serenity and insight are the path.
The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance are cessation.
These are the three truths.
In this regard, what is both arising and cessation?
Hope, longing, and delight, with cravings established among the manifold elements.
All longings, which originate from the root of ignorance,
have been brought to an end by me, together with their roots.
"Originate from the root of ignorance" refers to the origin [of suffering] according to the earlier teachers.
"All have been brought to an end by me, together with their roots"—this is cessation (*nirodha*).
These are the two truths.
The passage beginning "Through the non-awakening and non-penetration of four things" should be expanded in detail.
Of noble virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation:
therein, that which is the non-awakening and non-penetration of these four states is the origin;
the penetration of the conduit to existence is the cessation.
This is both origination and cessation.
In this regard, what is both origination and the path?
Those streams that exist in the world—
"O Ajita," said the Blessed One,
"mindfulness is their protection;
I call it the restraint of the streams."
"By means of wisdom these are closed up": this is the origin.
That which is wisdom and that which is mindfulness—this is the obstruction and the closing up; this is the path.
These are the two truths.
The Discourse on Volitional Action (*Sañcetaniya-sutta*) is explained through the simile of Daḷhanemi’s chariot over the course of six months.

In that context, whatever bodily action is crooked, defiled, and impure—whether it be the state of being crooked, the state of being defiled, or the state of being impure—this is the origin (*samudaya*).
In this way, verbal action and mental action are without crookedness, without hatred, and without impurity; that which is without crookedness, without hatred, and without impurity—this is the path.
Such are verbal action and mental action.
These two are the truths of the origin and the path.
In this context, what is the origin, the cessation, and the path?
"For one who is dependent there is wavering; for one who is independent there is no wavering. When there is no wavering, there is tranquility. When there is tranquility, there is no inclination.
When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going. When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and reappearing."
“...there is; when there is no passing away and rebirth, there is neither here nor beyond, nor in between the two.
This itself is the end of suffering.
In this context, these two dependencies constitute the origin.
That which is non-dependence and that which is non-coming-and-going—this is the path.
That which is the absence of coming and going, the absence of passing away and reappearing, and "this is the end of suffering"—this is cessation.
These are the three truths.
Mindfulness directed toward the body that is not established ...
[and so on] ... as for the knowledge and vision of liberation, this is the origin.
There are eleven supporting conditions for liberations, up to the full attainment of the supporting condition, wherein one dwells with mindfulness directed toward the body established.
Restraint by virtue is the path leading to peace; the knowledge and vision of liberation is the path;
and liberation itself is cessation.
These are the three truths.
The origin, the cessation, and the path.
In that regard, what is both cessation and the path?
It is by means of the truth accomplished by oneself.
Having attained Nibbāna by himself, having crossed over doubt,
and having understood non-existence in the world—
that bhikkhu has thus exhausted renewed existence.
That which is truth is this path;
that which is the exhaustion of renewed existence is cessation.
These are the two truths.
The five bases of liberation should be set forth in detail: "Either the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, or a certain wise fellow-celibate [teaches it].
For one who experiences the meaning [of that teaching], gladness arises; for one who is gladdened, rapture arises; ... down to ... becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate—this is the path.
That which is liberation is cessation.
Thus, the five bases for liberation have been explained in detail.
These two truths are cessation and the path.
These are the common suttas.
Having applied these common suttas—exactly as they are laid down—to other suttas by way of penetration and by way of characteristics, one should demonstrate them without omission.
Verses should be inferred from verses, and prose-expositions from prose-expositions.
These ten common augmentations and the single fourfold demonstration are common.
And this is the miscellaneous exposition.
One, five, and six; a portion of all, and the whole.
These two exclusions and the ten preceding ones.
These are the twelve augmentations of the truths.
To this extent, the entire discourse does not exist as such; it is either an exposition (*byākaraṇa*) or like a verse (*gāthā*).
One should not fail to enter into these twelve augmentations, but having searched with diligence, they must be demonstrated.
In this regard, here is the summary:
All suffering converges into seven points. Which seven?
Association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant— all suffering is to be demonstrated by these two terms.
Its two bases are the body and the mind.
Therefore it is said: "Bodily suffering and mental suffering. There is no suffering that is neither bodily nor mental; all suffering must be demonstrated by means of these two types of suffering:

the bodily and the mental. All suffering is comprised within three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*).
Thus, all that suffering is comprised within these three types of suffering.
Thus, this suffering is threefold.
Suffering is twofold: bodily and mental.
It is also twofold: association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant.
This is the sevenfold suffering.
Therein, the threefold origin is neither fourth nor fifth.
What is the threefold?
Craving, views, and karma.
Therein, craving is the origin of existence, and karma is likewise;
this is the origin of the inferiority and superiority of that which has been produced.
Thus, whatever inferiority and superiority there is among the destinations of existence, whatever is comprised by the three kinds of suffering,
and even this conscious body— which is produced from two roots for one shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving for existence—
that too is comprised by the three kinds of suffering.
Likewise, view (diṭṭhi) should be understood through the perversion (vipallāsa).
It should be demonstrated as sevenfold.
One perversion demonstrates three [of its aspects] and four bases of perversion (vipallāsavatthu).
In this context, what is the single perversion?
It is that perverted grasping which, by way of negation, constitutes an entry-point, such as grasping perversely that "the impermanent is permanent.
Thus are the four perversions.
This one [set] is perverted: perception, mind, and view.
What are the four bases of perversion?
The body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
Thus, for one who has fallen into perversion, unwholesomeness increases.
In this regard, perversion of perception increases hatred, the unwholesome root;
perversion of mind increases greed, the unwholesome root.
The perversion of view increases delusion, the unwholesome root.
Therein, the three wrongnesses are the fruit of hatred, the unwholesome root:
namely, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
The three wrongnesses are the fruit of the unwholesome root of greed:
wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration;
the two wrongnesses are the fruit of the unwholesome root of delusion: [wrong view and wrong speech].
Wrong view and wrong mindfulness.

Thus, the unwholesome is with cause and with condition; the perversions are the conditions, and the unwholesome roots are the causes. These very factors, neither less nor more, are to be demonstrated by two conditions.
In the case of cessation and the path, taking the perversions as the basis, there are four [factors] further on by way of their opposites.
In this regard, there are these summary verses:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance,
The mind, and also the fetters.”
With the craving for existence severed,
there are these two kinds of liberation.
This body is like a water jar.
Abandon that which is not yours;
whatever sorrows and lamentations there may be,
such as those of Timbaruka, are all self-made.
Suffering, views that have arisen,
and that which is like the cowherd’s simile—
let there be mindfulness directed toward the body.
Tranquility and insight,
hope, longing, and delight— the non-comprehension of these four things.
Whatever streams there are in the world,
they are like the firm rim of a wheel;
for one who relies on them, there is wavering.
One who has not established mindfulness directed to the body is liberated through truth realized by oneself and through the bases of liberation.

In the *Peṭakopadesa*, spoken by Mahākaccāyana, this is the first section, titled "The Exposition of the Noble Truths," which was [previously] taught by the Blessed One while living, by the Tathāgata who is like an ocean for those such as myself.
